planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina Sweetheart is grown chiefly for its dramatic tricolor spring foliage rather than for fruit or vegetable production, so no direct-sow schedule applies.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade in the hottest zones to keep leaf color from fading. Carolina Sweetheart was bred at North Carolina State University and is best known for spring foliage that emerges deep burgundy-purple splashed with hot pink and creamy white, a striking tricolor combination that gradually settles to green edged in white as the leaves mature through summer. Typical rosy-pink pea-shaped flowers appear on bare branches in early spring ahead of the foliage display, followed by the usual redbud seed pods. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or damaged wood right after flowering, and site it where the ever-changing leaf coloration can be viewed up close, such as near a patio or garden entrance.

common_name: Don Egolf Chinese Redbud (Dwarf Compact Rounded Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Don Egolf stays naturally small and dense, so it needs far less space than a standard Eastern redbud and suits foundation plantings or small-garden specimens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing room for its dense, uniformly rounded habit to develop without crowding. Don Egolf was selected and introduced by the U.S. National Arboretum, honoring plant breeder Donald Egolf, and is valued for producing an unusually heavy floral display of rosy-purple pea-like flowers packed along its branches in early spring, followed by glossy dark green, heart-shaped foliage that holds its color well through summer. It rarely sets viable seed, so bloom energy channels into an exceptionally full flowering show rather than into pod production. Prune only lightly to remove dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since its naturally tidy, compact form needs little corrective shaping.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy permanent arbor, trellis, or trained standard form able to support its eventual weight.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy support, training the twining stems along a permanent structure or as a trained standard. Issai, whose name references its unusually young flowering age, is prized among Japanese wisteria selections for blooming within just a few years of planting rather than the decade or more typical of seed-grown wisteria, producing fragrant violet-blue racemes in mid-spring. Its earlier, more reliable bloom habit makes it a popular choice for gardeners who want flowering wisteria without a long establishment wait, including for container and bonsai culture. Prune back long whippy summer growth after flowering and again in late winter to encourage the short flowering spurs that carry next year's blooms, and watch for root suckers and self-seeding since Asian wisteria species can naturalize aggressively in warm, humid regions.

common_name: Blue Danube Camassia (Deep Blue Large-Flowered Camas)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Blue Danube is a deeper, richer violet-blue selection than the typical species, chosen for its saturated flower color rather than any difference in habit.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing them 8-12 inches apart to allow clumps to bulk up over time. Blue Danube produces tall, densely packed spikes of star-shaped flowers in a deeper, more saturated violet-blue than the typical species, opening from the bottom of the spike upward over several weeks in mid to late spring. Like other camassia, it tolerates wet spring soil far better than most bulbs but appreciates a drier dormancy through summer, making it a good match for meadow plantings, rain gardens, or the back of a moist perennial border. Leave the strappy foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps only occasionally, once flowering begins to decline after many years.

common_name: Ivory Bells Persian Fritillary (Cream-White Persian Fritillaria)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in sharply well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in a warm, sheltered full-sun spot in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; Ivory Bells substitutes soft cream-white flowers for the deep plum-purple of the typical species.

directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in sharply well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun in fall, since standing winter moisture quickly rots the bulbs of this Middle Eastern native. Ivory Bells is a striking pale selection of Persian fritillary, its stout, upright 24-36 inch stems clothed in glaucous grey-green leaves and topped with a long raceme of 20-30 pendant, bell-shaped flowers in a soft ivory to pale cream rather than the smoky plum-purple of the species, giving a lighter, more luminous effect in the border. It combines beautifully with dark tulips or deep-purple ornamental alliums for contrast, and like all Persian fritillaries it may take two or three seasons to settle in and flower at full strength. Provide a raised bed or extra grit in gardens with wet winters, and leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom.

planting.note: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; planting on the side keeps water from pooling in the bulb's hollow crown and causing rot.

directions: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, since standing water in the hollow-crowned bulb quickly causes rot. Aurora is a classic orange-red crown imperial selection, producing a dramatic, tall flower stalk topped with a whorl of large, nodding, bell-shaped orange-red blooms beneath a tuft of leafy green bracts, similar in scale to 'Rubra Maxima' but with a brighter, warmer tone. The whole plant carries a musky, skunk-like scent that most gardeners find unpleasant up close, but which usefully deters deer, voles, and other bulb-eating pests from the bed. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering, and avoid dividing or moving established clumps, since crown imperial resents disturbance and may sulk for a season or two afterward.

common_name: Aphrodite Snake's Head Fritillary (Large Round White Checkered Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall as soon as available, since the small fleshy bulbs dry out quickly, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Aphrodite bears larger, more rounded pure white bells than the ordinary 'Alba' form.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall as soon as available, since the small, fleshy bulbs lose viability quickly in storage; site in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, ideally in a damp meadow or streamside planting. Aphrodite is a robust white-flowered selection of snake's head fritillary, distinguished from the more common 'Alba' by noticeably larger, rounder, more substantial nodding bells held on slender wiry stems above narrow grassy foliage. It naturalizes readily in moisture-retentive soil, spreading gradually by offsets and self-sown seed to form generous colonies over the years, and looks especially effective massed together with the checkered purple species form. Allow the foliage to die back and yellow naturally after flowering before cutting it back.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this East Asian species naturalizes readily and self-sows in favorable sites.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Native to China and long naturalized in Japan, Thunberg's fritillary sends up slender stems clothed in narrow, twining-tipped leaves and topped with several nodding, pale yellowish-green bells faintly checkered inside, opening in early to mid spring ahead of most other fritillaries. It is easier and more vigorous in the garden than many showier species in the genus, bulking up steadily and self-sowing where happy, and the bulb has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine as 'zhe bei mu.' Let the foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom before cutting it down, and divide congested clumps in late summer dormancy only when flowering starts to decline.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun; this Central Asian species needs a warm, dry summer dormancy to thrive and is well suited to a rock garden or bulb frame.

directions: Plant small bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, gritty, humus-rich soil in full sun, ideally on a slope or raised bed that stays dry over summer. Native to rocky slopes and scree in the mountains of Central Asia, Bukhara fritillary is a diminutive, charming species bearing several small, upward-facing to slightly nodding white star-shaped flowers marked with green on the outside, held just above narrow, glossy foliage in early spring. It is a good candidate for a rock garden, trough, or alpine bulb frame where its need for a hot, dry summer rest can be met more reliably than in an ordinary border, and it multiplies steadily by offsets once established in a well-suited spot. Allow the foliage to die back completely and keep the site on the dry side through summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall, or divide and move clumps 'in the green' just after flowering, into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; Three Ships is prized for reliably opening its first flowers around Christmas, weeks ahead of most other snowdrops.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Three Ships is one of the earliest snowdrop cultivars to bloom, traditionally opening its first honey-scented, rounded white flowers around Christmas Day, considerably ahead of the main snowdrop season in late winter. Like other Galanthus plicatus selections, it has broad, folded-back leaf margins that distinguish it from Galanthus nivalis even before flowering, and it bulks up at a steady pace into worthwhile clumps. Divide congested clumps in the green immediately after bloom and replant promptly, since the bulbs dislike prolonged drying out of the roots.

common_name: Mrs Macnamara Snowdrop (Vigorous Early-Flowering Hybrid Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mrs Macnamara is valued for flowering unusually early and for its exceptional vigor compared to most named snowdrop cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally under deciduous trees or shrubs. Mrs Macnamara is a robust hybrid snowdrop believed to derive from Galanthus elwesii and Galanthus plicatus parentage, prized for flowering weeks ahead of most other snowdrops and for its exceptional vigor and broad, blue-grey foliage, which bulks up into generous clumps faster than many named cultivars. Its large, rounded, honey-scented flowers make it a reliable, easy choice for gardeners wanting an early, distinctive snowdrop that establishes quickly. Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green for the best transplant success.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense superhots germinate slowly and need sustained warmth to break dormancy.

directions: 7 Pot Bubblegum is a Trinidad-origin selection prized for smooth, slightly bumpy orange pods that ripen from pale green through a distinctive salmon-pink stage before finishing deep orange. Growers favor it for a fruitier, less acrid heat than many 7 Pot strains, with fragrance reminiscent of tropical fruit alongside the scorching capsaicin load. Give plants a long warm season and consistent moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and misshapen pods on this variety. Cage or stake mature plants, as heavy fruit clusters can snap brittle branches in wind.

common_name: Yellow Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Yellow Ghost Pepper)

planting.note: Sow indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost date; bhut jolokia types are slow to germinate and sulk in cool soil.

directions: Yellow Bhut Jolokia is a bright lemon-to-gold-podded phenotype of the classic Northeast Indian ghost pepper, with the same characteristically wrinkled, thin-walled fruit and searing heat as the red strain. Some growers report a slightly fruitier, less smoky flavor than red bhut jolokia, making it popular for hot sauces where a lighter color is desired. Provide full sun, rich well-drained soil, and even watering, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under moisture stress. Wear gloves when handling ripe pods, as the oils cling stubbornly to skin.

common_name: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Chocolate Ghost Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat; pods need a long, hot season to fully darken to chocolate-brown.

directions: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia is a dark-podded strain of the classic ghost pepper, ripening through green and reddish-brown before settling into a deep, glossy chocolate color. It carries the same wrinkled pod texture and formidable heat as red bhut jolokia, with a slightly earthier, roasted undertone favored by hot sauce makers. Because the fruit colors up slowly, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture to extend the ripening window. Keep soil evenly moist and handle harvested pods with gloves.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Peach Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Peach Ghost Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; germination is slow and uneven below 80F soil temperature.

directions: Peach Bhut Jolokia ripens to a warm apricot-peach hue instead of the classic red, on the same wrinkled, thin-fleshed pods and blistering heat associated with ghost peppers. Growers often note a subtly sweeter, fruitier aroma compared to red strains, though the Scoville load remains firmly in superhot territory. Give plants full sun, rich well-drained soil, and consistent watering to avoid blossom drop during fruit set. Use gloves when harvesting and processing pods, since capsaicin oils are persistent on skin.

planting.note: Start indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this strain is distinct from the red Butch T scorpion and needs a full hot season to ripen.

directions: Chocolate Trinidad Scorpion produces the same tailed, stinger-tipped pods as the classic red scorpion strains, but ripens to a rich mahogany brown with a deeper, more smoky flavor beneath the intense heat. It is a separate color strain from Butch T and Moruga lines, grown by superhot collectors for hot sauce and extract use. Provide a long warm season, steady moisture, and staking once fruit clusters get heavy, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under water stress. Handle ripe pods with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Stewartstonian is a classic Gable hybrid prized as much for its wine-red winter foliage as for its spring bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Stewartstonian is a Joseph Gable-bred hybrid azalea named for his Pennsylvania nursery town, bearing single brick-red to red-orange flowers in a dense mid-spring flush over a naturally mounding, twiggy habit. Its standout trait is foliage that shifts to a rich maroon-red through fall and winter before greening back up in spring, giving it multi-season interest well beyond the bloom period. Water deeply during dry spells while roots establish, mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds set soon after petals drop.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Herbert is a long-popular Gable hybrid valued for its reddish-purple hose-in-hose flowers and reliable cold hardiness.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Herbert is one of Joseph Gable's most enduring hybrid azaleas, opening reddish-purple hose-in-hose flowers in a heavy mid-spring flush over a dense, rounded, semi-evergreen mound. Its combination of cold hardiness, compact form, and long garden history has kept it a mainstay alongside Stewartstonian among older Gable-hybrid selections still widely sold today. Water deeply during dry spells while establishing, mulch to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature, and prune immediately after flowering since next season's buds form shortly after bloom.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
